title: One fine night
hook: don't chase the past, don't pin hopes on the future; see what is here, today
carry: see it clearly, right where it is

segments.voice: Yesterday: devaduta, the messengers of the gods: a baby, an elder, someone sick, someone punished, a body. Your line: the messengers came.

Ten minutes in old photos pulls the mood one way. Ten minutes planning next year pulls it another. In both, the room you're sitting in has gone missing. The hundred and thirty-first discourse is short, and at its heart is a verse of just a few lines. The Buddha recites it at Jeta's Grove near Savatthi, then explains it. And it won't stay in one discourse: the next three come back to it.
screen: `TEN MINUTES IN OLD PHOTOS.` → `TEN MINUTES IN NEXT YEAR.` → `A SHORT VERSE, EXPLAINED.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Don't chase after the past. Don't build your hopes on the future. The past is already left behind; the future hasn't come. Whatever is present, see it clearly, right where it is, steady and unshaken. Do today what needs doing, with energy. Who knows, death may come tomorrow, and there's no bargaining with death and his great army. Whoever lives this way, keen, day and night, the peaceful sage calls one who has had a bhaddekaratta. Bhadda means good or auspicious. Eka means one. Ratta is the hard part: it's usually read as night, but translators don't agree on the whole, so you'll find one fine night, a single excellent night, or an auspicious day. The shape of the teaching is clear, though. The Buddha explains how people chase the past: I had such a body, such feelings, such thoughts, and they find delight there. How they build hopes on the future: I'll have such a body, such feelings. And how, in the present, they take body or feeling or mind as a self, and get pulled along. The one who doesn't is the one having that fine night. Not a night of special visions. A night, or a day, lived where it actually is. After yesterday's messengers, this is the answer: not fear, but full attention to the only day there is.
screen: `DON'T CHASE THE PAST` · `DON'T PIN HOPES ON THE FUTURE` · `SEE WHAT IS HERE, TODAY` · `BHADDA, EKA, RATTA` · then, large: `ONE FINE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit a while, and each time the mind slides into a memory, say softly: past; each time it jumps to a plan: future. Then come back to what's actually here: this breath, this sound, this weight. You don't have to hate the past or the future; you're just choosing, for now, the room you're in.
Bhaddekaratta. One fine night, an auspicious day: not chasing the past, not hoping on the future, seeing what's here clearly, today. Today's word.
Your line: see it clearly, right where it is. No special visions needed, just this one day, lived. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The bhaddekaratta verse is chanted in some Theravada monasteries, and meditation teachers in several traditions use it to teach dwelling in the present moment.

original.note: Pali bhaddekaratta: bhadda, good; eka, one; ratta, perhaps night. its exact sense is debated.
